title: 1  Deep structures: a world without a centre
section: Reading the period: the four questions
text:
Reading the period: the four questions
The three thousand years from about 3500 to 500 BCE can be put through the same four questions that drive the rest of this book, with the warning that the answers here are softer than any later chapter’s, because the evidence is thinner and the system looser. They are worth running all the same, because this is where the questions themselves are forged. The first question was about direction, and the answer is that the system did both, repeatedly, with no single arc running through the period. The three cycles narrated above — the Uruk sphere, the Gulf trade, the Late Bronze Age palace economies — each integrated and then came apart, which is the module’s rhythm in miniature. The lesson the sequence bequeathed to every later chapter is that integration bred fragility: the routes that carried trade also carried shocks, and a more connected system was a more exposed one. The Collapse of 1177 BCE is the clearest instance in the book, because the palace economies that failed together were the most tightly coupled thing the ancient world had built.46
46 Sources: Scott (Page 1199); Kriwaczek (Page 72); Cline (Loc 507). Read more: Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014).47 Sources: Cunliffe (Loc 158, 909); Frahm (Page 47); Anthony (Loc 6829); Cline (Loc 1646). Read more: Cunliffe, By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean (2015).The second question was about channels, and this period’s answer is that all three of the module’s corridors were born here at once: the maritime Indian Ocean, the desert and oasis route that would later be called the Silk Road, and the great Eurasian steppe. Of the three, the steppe was the era’s dynamic engine rather than its periphery, a band of unbroken grass running some seven thousand kilometres from eastern Europe to the Great Wall of China. The ocean, the corridor this book centres on, was still largely waiting, its monsoon geography laid down but its traffic thin. To see how the channels actually worked it helps to follow one good, and the most revealing is tin. Bronze, the period’s defining metal, needed it, yet tin lay almost nowhere near the cities that used it, so it had to travel long distances to reach them — and its price marked the route, in barter ratios that the cuneiform records preserve centuries before any coin existed to express them. The volumes were not trivial either: a single cargo such as the one lost off Uluburun around 1300 BCE carried perhaps a tonne of tin in one hull.47






ImportantFollow the money



With no coins yet, the period’s bullion tracer was the relative price of metals, and tin is the clearest one to track. It had to travel because bronze needed it and it lay far from the cities that consumed it. The gap between its price at Assur, about 6.7 shekels of silver per 100 shekels of tin, and in Anatolia, about 14.3, moved the metal from where it was cheap toward where it was dear, centuries before coinage. The gap is also a measurement: roughly a doubling over 950 kilometres is what carriage cost in this technology, and later chapters watch that wedge narrow. On the Introduction’s test — a gap bounded by the cost of carriage — that makes Assur and Kanesh about as integrated as the technology of the day allowed, and the measure of later integration is not that such gaps disappear but that they shrink toward the physical cost of carriage. This is the same “follow the metal” logic the module will use for millennia to locate the centre, except that here it shows up in barter ratios scratched onto clay rather than in the output of any mint.








Figure 1.10: The price of distance: 100 shekels of tin cost about 6.7 shekels of silver at Assur but about 14.3 in Anatolia, where it was scarcer. The gap is not arbitrage — it is the cost of carriage, quoted, centuries before any coin existed to express it, and integration is that wedge narrowing (stylised; values from the Old Assyrian records). Source: Frahm.









Figure 1.11: A single Bronze Age cargo as a dataset of one: the Uluburun wreck (c.1300 BCE) carried ~10 tonnes of copper and ~1 tonne of tin — the ~10:1 bronze recipe — plus glass, resin, ivory and amber, with products of at least nine or ten cultures. Bulk metal moved by sea long before coins (estimated tonnages). Source: Cline.



The third question was about modes: what crossed the connection? Two kinds of thing did, and the chapter is clearer if they are kept apart. On one side are real flows, and the production function names them: output itself moves as goods, useful knowledge as technique, people as labour, produced assets as capital. On the other side run monetary and financial flows, things that settle a transaction and claims that carry purchasing power across time. Silver sits on both sides at once, which is the complication this period is best at teaching. The evidence for each is a different instrument. Goods are somebody else’s land, arriving in usable form. A cargo of tin is a mineral endowment that Mesopotamia did not have, and that is what makes tin and not grain the story: a small flow of an input nothing can substitute for has more structural consequence than a large flow of something anybody can grow. High-value processed goods travelled too, and mattered out of proportion to their bulk, because a supply that could not easily be expanded met a demand that would pay almost anything — Ugarit paid its yearly tribute to the Hittites not only in gold but in dyed wool and finished garments, cloth being among the most concentrated stores of value a Bronze Age economy could ship, and the Tyrian purple described above is the vivid later case.
There is also one piece of evidence here for the other side of the equation, and the archaeology of trade almost never reaches it: demand. Ancient proteins recovered from dental calculus at Bronze Age Megiddo, around 1650 to 1320 BCE, record what individual people actually put in their mouths — cereals, sesame and dates as expected, and then soybean in one individual, turmeric in one, probable banana in one. At least one person in the second-millennium Levant ate a South Asian spice and a South Asian pulse. What that licenses is narrow. It establishes contact and is silent on commerce; it cannot say how many, how often, or whether a market existed, and every exotic in the study rests on a single person. The study’s authors read it less cautiously than this and write of a pattern of established trade, and the gap between what evidence licenses and what is claimed from it, including by the people who produced it, is worth more to an economist than the finding.48
48 Sources: Scott et al. (2021) on the Megiddo and Tel Erani dental calculus; the identifications rest on two and three peptides respectively, at or barely above the standard authentication threshold; Cline (Loc 2308) on Ugarit’s tribute in cloth. Note: there is no published rebuttal of these identifications — the caution here is this book’s reading of a general methodological standard, not a critique in the literature. Read more: Scott et al., “Exotic foods reveal contact between South Asia and the Near East”, PNAS 118 (2021).Technology moved, and it moved slowly. The chariot took something like eight hundred years to cross a continent, from Sintashta graves east of the Urals before 2000 BCE to China around 1200, and that is the diffusion speed of this world. People moved, and two studies measure it in a way no document can. The Harappan cemeteries are the first. Strontium and lead isotopes in tooth enamel, seventy-seven teeth from fifty-five individuals at Harappa and Farmana, and the design is what makes the result strong: the three molars form at different ages, so one skeleton yields an ordered sequence of childhood residences rather than an average. First molars fall outside the local range; second and third converge on it, at Farmana around three to five years of age. These were first-generation immigrants. The economics is in where they came from. The migrants point north-west to the upper Indus and north-east to the Punjab plains, and the lead in the Farmana burials points at the Khetri copper belt about a hundred and fifty kilometres south, so migrants and metals travelled the same corridors. Resource peripheries exported the material and the people who knew how to get it, which is a relationship this chapter meets again at its far end, in Cornwall.
The sample will not carry a migration rate, and the reason is a selection rule rather than a small sample size: fewer than six hundred Indus skeletons exist from a century of excavation across some 680,000 square kilometres, and formal cemetery burial is rare within that. A cemetery here is a complete sample of a small institution rather than a thin random sample of Indus society.49 The second study is in Britain, and it measures a flow of people with no price attached to it at all. Five isotope systems run on 131 pigs from four Late Neolithic henge complexes in southern Britain, around 2800 to 2400 BCE, and the strontium range at Durrington Walls is wider than at any other published British site, wider than a Roman legionary fortress sitting on far more varied geology, while three kilometres away Middle Neolithic animals from West Amesbury Farm show the narrowest range of any British assemblage. So the wide catchment is not a property of the landscape; it is new, and it is institutional. The economics turns on the animal, because pigs drive badly over distance and there is no reason to walk one for hundreds of kilometres rather than carry the meat, unless the animal and the people who raised it are meant to arrive together. The isotopes are therefore measuring the geographic reach of a mobilisation organised without money, writing, prices or a market. Hold it in mind for the fourth question: peripheral in a network is not the same thing as simple.50
49 Sources: Valentine et al. (2015) on strontium and lead isotopes at Harappa and Farmana. Caveats the authors state: the local range is defined from faunal samples whose spread suggests some of the animals were themselves imported, which makes the non-local verdict conservative but is an inference; breastfeeding by immigrant mothers and childhood exposure to imported lead-bearing cosmetics are argued against rather than eliminated; the South Asian ore and slag reference data are in the authors’ own word equivocal. Read more: Valentine et al., PLOS ONE 10 (2015).50 Sources: Madgwick et al. (2019), the largest fully published multi-isotope faunal dataset in archaeology. Caveat: provenance here is by exclusion — the animals are shown not to be local, not traced to farms — and with thin British comparative data for sulfur and oxygen, most of the geographic weight rests on strontium. Read more: Madgwick et al., Science Advances 5 (2019).Capital was present and thin. Ships, pack animals, irrigation works, workshops and stores are the capital of this world, and there is nothing in it that could be called a capital market. That point needs care, because finance in this period was sophisticated without being broad, and the two are easy to confuse. Money and credit are not capital; they are what let capital be assembled and what bridges the delay between committing resources and getting them back. That delay is the thing to picture: perhaps a hundred days between committing goods at Assur and seeing any silver return, with the donkeys, fodder, drivers and tolls all paid for in advance. A trade with that shape cannot run on cash in hand. So it ran on credit, and we know it did because the Kanesh archive is a merchant archive: some twelve thousand private letters and account tablets from the trading families themselves rather than from a palace.
For once in this period we are reading the traders, and the claims and obligations in those letters are denominated in silver, across households and across a political frontier, with no coin anywhere in the system. The institutional depth goes back further. Interest-bearing debt is securely attested from the later third millennium and may reach to about 3000 BCE, and rulers periodically wiped the slate: the earliest recorded is Enmetena of Lagash, around 2400 BCE, and the Sumerian word for what he granted was amargi, literally a return to the mother, debtors going home. It is the earliest attested word for freedom in any written language, and the first freedom in the written record is freedom from debt.
One last flow belongs here, and it complicates this book’s own spine before the spine has started. Before coinage, silver in the Levant circulated as hacksilver, cut and weighed, and because it was not endlessly remelted its lead-isotope signature reads onto the ore field that was worked. Seventy-five items from three dated Phoenician hoards show the source moving: Anatolian silver is prominent in the tenth and ninth centuries, but by the ninth-century hoard at Ein Hofez only two of twenty-nine items are consistent with Anatolian ore and most point to Iberia. The metal is running west to east. The expectation set up by Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 is that silver flows toward Asia. The first traceable flow in the record does the opposite. Direction is a function of where the ore sits and where the demand sits, and both of those move.51 The fourth question was about Europe, and this is the answer that has changed most. The old line was that Bronze Age Europe sat outside the world system whose cores were in West Asia and the Indian Ocean. That is not right, and the thing that changed it is tin. The obstacle had never been the artefacts but the absence of a reference base: nobody had characterised the ores, so there was nothing to compare an ingot against. A Durham-led programme built one, and the discrimination runs in two steps.
51 Sources: Eshel et al. (2019) on lead isotopes in hacksilver from Dor, Akko and Ein Hofez; Frahm (Page 47) and Goetzmann (loc 592, 836) on Old Assyrian credit; Graeber (Loc 8075, 4560) on the amargi cancellations; Barjamovic, Chaney, Cosar and Hortacsu (2019), QJE 134(3), on the Kanesh corpus. Caveats: many hacksilver items are mixtures rather than single-source, and copper-alloyed hoards were excluded from the study, which is a selection rule of unknown direction. Graeber’s wider debt-before-barter thesis is contested; the specific Mesopotamian facts here are not, and Goetzmann is the safer citation for the finance-history framing. Read more: Goetzmann, Money Changes Everything (2016).52 Sources: Williams et al. (2025) for the Durham ore programme, the indium discrimination and the model ages; Powell et al. (2022) for the Taurus and Musiston attribution of 105 Uluburun ingots; Berger et al. (2023) for the indium measurements that cut against the Cornish reading of that cargo. Worth knowing: Berger is a co-author on two of the three, so the lines of evidence are less independent than they look, and lead-isotope provenancing at Uluburun is compromised by lead contamination running from 22 ppm to 11.5 per cent. Read more: Williams et al. (2025).Cornish and Devon cassiterites carry up to 176 parts per million of indium where Iberian and French ores are under ten, and indium survives smelting, which is what makes it readable on an ingot rather than on a rock; that removes Iberia and France. Lead-isotope model age then separates the two survivors, the Erzgebirge coming out at 318 to 323 million years against Cornwall and Devon at 274 to 293, and tin from three radiocarbon-dated Israeli wrecks gives 290. One sentence keeps that honest in a seminar: tin isotopes alone cannot do this job, because the tin provinces overlap too much, and the work is done by indium and by lead-isotope model age. What is settled is the Cornish case for those wrecks. What is not settled is Uluburun, where two laboratories read the same cargo and reach incompatible answers, one programme putting the ingots inside Cornish and Devon ranges and another attributing roughly two-thirds to the Taurus and a third to Central Asia, three thousand kilometres east. Concede the strongest point against the Cornish reading rather than smoothing it: the Uluburun ingots measure 2 to 7 parts per million of indium against up to 176 in Cornish ore, and indium is the discriminator. The verdict here rests on the Israeli wrecks.52
So the answer is not “peripheral” in the sense students expect. Britain supplied tin, without which there is no bronze, to a network whose demand, capital, weights, writing and organisation all sat in West Asia. That is a resource periphery inside the system, which is a different thing from being outside it, and the production model is what makes “periphery” precise rather than dismissive. The tin came from decentralised small alluvial workings, worked part-time alongside farming, handed to coastal trading places and passed down the line. There was no direct contact of any kind between Britain and the Levant: nobody in Cornwall knew where the metal ended up and nobody in Ugarit knew where it started. Britain supplied an input; it did not organise, price or capture the trade in it. Which is this chapter’s sharpest instance of N as power, and the pattern recurs at Potosi, at Banda and at every commodity exporter in the twentieth century: the holder of the scarce resource was not the holder of the rents.
The scale needs care. Perhaps 100 to 200 tonnes of tin a year across all of Europe and the Mediterranean in the mid-second millennium BCE — and say the caveat in the same breath, because the authors call the figure speculative. It is scaled from copper output at three mines on an assumed ten per cent tin-to-copper ratio, then extrapolated across more than a hundred known mines, and a number built by multiplying an uncertain quantity by an assumed coefficient inherits the uncertainty of both. For proportion: Cornwall and Devon produced about 400 tonnes a year in 1200 CE on substantially the same technology with some six thousand mainly part-time workers. A strategic flow, then, and not a large one. None of which makes Europe simple. Varna on the Black Sea, around 4500 BCE, yielded some three thousand gold objects weighing roughly six kilograms, more gold than every other fifth-millennium find in the world put together, and the Durrington pigs above show the same island mobilising animals across most of its length to one place. Organisational sophistication and peripheral position are independent facts, and this period has both. Behind all four questions stood the forces this module tracks: geography came first, with the Himalayan uplift, the monsoon and the great rivers setting the board; climate was the first dynamic driver, its swings bearing on the rise and fall of cores; and technology — the sail married to monsoon knowledge, the horse, the wheel, bronze — turned geographic possibility into movement.53
53 Sources: on scale and the production model, Williams et al. (2025); Anthony (Loc 3941) on Varna; Madgwick et al. (2019) on the Durrington catchment. Read more: Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

title: 1  Deep structures: a world without a centre
text:
Which input was binding?
Every chapter in this book closes its analysis with the same line of the ledger: which input was doing the work, and which one was in the way? N was binding everywhere, and it bound in two different ways. As a level, there was no tin in Mesopotamia and Uruk hauled its stone eighty kilometres, so a bronze-using city had to be connected to a continent whether it wanted to be or not. As variance, the river under the Indus cities was not short of water so much as unreliable about it. Two kinds of scarcity, one input, and the second is the one students miss. A moved, and moved slowest, at eight hundred years for the chariot to cross a continent. L was the residual claimant, since a better technique or a windfall of land was captured as more people rather than as higher income per head, which is Malthus written in this book’s notation and why the period’s thriving is counted in cities and populations. K was real but thin, and finance was sophisticated without being broad: credit crossed a political frontier at Assur and Kanesh centuries before anyone struck a coin, and it was relationship-based, running between known households and named agents, with nothing in this world resembling an impersonal capital market. And control of N is where the economic power sat, with Dilmun taking a cut at a chokepoint without producing anything, Cyprus with its copper and Cornwall with its tin. Britain had the tin; West Asia had the trade.

title: 1  Deep structures: a world without a centre
section: The verdict: where was the centre?
text:
The verdict: where was the centre?
The verdict for this period is that there was no single centre, and it is delivered with low confidence by design. What the evidence shows is several loosely linked riverine cores rather than one integrated world economy with a weight that can be located. The Near East, and Uruk above all, was the most central node, a large urban demand pole and the supplier of metals into the long-distance trade. The Indus led the Gulf trade through its mature phase, and it survives as a bright spot in a thin record rather than as a documented centre. Which way that thinness cuts matters. Because the humid tropics destroy organic evidence, what survives from the Indus is a lower bound on its activity rather than an estimate of it, which licenses a claim about direction and nothing about magnitude. What it does not license is treating the sparseness of the record as though it were evidence for the argument, a move this chapter made in an earlier draft and should not make. Egypt and the forming East Asian core sat largely apart from the western-Eurasian system that the evidence actually documents.54
54 Sources: Scott (Page 805); Frahm (Page 46). Read more: Frahm, Assyria (2023).55 Sources: Pearson (Ch.1) on the monsoon deep structure and the channels; Scott (Page 631) on the agrarian denominator. Read more: Pearson, The Indian Ocean (2003).The centre-of-gravity question that runs through the rest of the book is therefore not yet applicable. This period neither supports nor contradicts the claim that Asia was central, because it predates a connected system in which a centre of gravity is a meaningful idea. The first chapter at which the question becomes answerable is the next one, when Alexander and the Achaemenid inheritance fuse the channels into something like a single trans-Eurasian system. What this chapter contributes is structural rather than evidential: it lays down the monsoon and the channel geography that will later make the Indian Ocean the natural integrator. Two cautions govern how the period’s own thriving should be read. The denominator has to be kept honest, since these were overwhelmingly agrarian subsistence economies in which the great majority farmed and never handled a trade good, and the long-distance traffic described here was a thin and lucrative network laid over that mass rather than the bulk of output. And whatever thriving the period shows was measured in numbers rather than income per head: more food meant more people rather than richer people, the Malthusian condition humanity shared with every other species. The switch from measuring an economy by its scale to measuring it by the living standards of the people in it lies far ahead, at the Great Divergence of Chapter 7.55






WarningThe debate: how much weight should geography carry?



Cunliffe, and Diamond before him, lean hard on geography as the deciding force — the mountains and monsoon and grass corridors setting what was possible. The counter stresses human agency and contingency, the choices that geography permitted but did not dictate. The climate-collapse story is contested in the same way. The 4.2 ka weakening of the monsoon is invoked behind the Harappan decline, and drought behind the Late Bronze Age Collapse, yet the palaeo-record does not cleanly show a sharp, sustained drought at the right moment, so mono-causal climate accounts overreach. The sensible posture is to hold both at once: deep structures shaped the board on which the period was played, but people still chose the moves. Name the positions, weigh them, and leave the question genuinely open.


Data exhibit — the Uluburun cargo, a dataset of one. With almost no quantitative records, a single well-excavated shipwreck does the work that a price series does in later chapters. The cargo is itemised above, and Figure 1.11 plots the two metals. What you could do with this: infer how many separate economies one hull implicates, and ask what the copper-to-tin ratio implies about where the metals were sourced and where the bronze was to be made — reasoning from one rich object to a whole system, with the uncertainty stated.

title: 1  Deep structures: a world without a centre
text:
Threads forward
What this chapter hands on is a period fully described rather than a verdict: a world of loosely linked riverine cores, three cycles of integration and collapse, and the first evidence that connection carries shocks as well as goods. That last lesson runs from the Late Bronze Age Collapse through every later disintegration the book meets. The hand-off to the next chapter is geographic and institutional at once. By about 500 BCE the Achaemenid empire had reunited the Near East, iron had loosened the tin bottleneck, and coinage had begun to standardise money. Alexander is where it turns, and the three channels born here would fuse into the first genuinely trans-Eurasian world system — Rome, Parthia, the Kushans and Han China strung along the routes — with the monsoon road this chapter laid down as its maritime spine and India at the fulcrum. At that point, for the first time, “where did the weight sit?” becomes a question the evidence can answer.56
56 Sources: Scott (Page 631); Cline (Loc 507) on the fragility lesson. Citation withdrawn: the Achaemenid reunification, iron and early coinage claim was attributed to Cline, 1177 B.C., but that book does not discuss the Achaemenid reunification and the word “coinage” does not appear in it; the claim needs a source that carries it. Schaps, The Invention of Coinage and the Monetization of Ancient Greece (2004), covers the coinage half. Read more: Findlay & O’Rourke, Power and Plenty (2007).

Classic research: the foundations
The questions this chapter raises — was Bronze Age trade a market or a redistribution; how much weight should geography carry — descend from a bench of historians, archaeologists and anthropologists.

Polanyi (ed., 1957), Trade and Market in the Early Empires — the substantivist thesis that early “trade” was administered and redistributive rather than market exchange. The reference point for this chapter’s central debate; the recent cliometric work below is the market-side rebuttal. Pair them.
Algaze (1993; 2008), The Uruk World System and Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization — the “Uruk world system” and the early peak-and-contraction that predates the Gulf trade.
Adams (1981), Heartland of Cities — the classic survey-archaeology of Mesopotamian urbanisation and settlement.
Sherratt (1981), “Plough and Pastoralism: Aspects of the Secondary Products Revolution,” in Pattern of the Past — the traction/wool/dairy thesis; teach as contested (discrete event vs gradual adoption).
Possehl (2002), The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective — the standard synthesis and the “transformation, not collapse” reading of the Harappan decline.
Anthony (2007), The Horse, the Wheel, and Language — horse domestication, the Sintashta chariot, and the Indo-European expansions; the steppe-as-engine story.
Cline (2014), 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed — the systemic-fragility reading of the Late Bronze Age Collapse; this chapter’s first “integration creates fragility” case.
Graeber (2011), Debt: The First 5,000 Years — credit, debt and the amargi cancellations; the case that finance preceded coinage.

section: At the research frontier: recent cliometric work
text:
At the research frontier: recent cliometric work
A striking amount of recent economics reaches back into deep prehistory — fitting trade models to cuneiform tablets, and testing the origins of states, farming and the Malthusian regime. Every entry verified.

Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019), “Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(3): 1455–1503 — a structural gravity model fit to ~12,000 Old Assyrian merchant tablets from Kanesh that recovers trade costs and even triangulates the locations of lost cities. The chapter’s proof that Bronze Age long-distance trade was a genuine, estimable market. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009]
Mayshar, Moav & Pascali (2022), “The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability?” Journal of Political Economy 130(4): 1091–1144 — hierarchy and taxation arose from the appropriability of storable cereals, not from higher farm productivity; the institutional micro-foundation under the riverine cores. [DOI 10.1086/718372]
Matranga (2024), “The Ant and the Grasshopper: Seasonality and the Invention of Agriculture,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(3): 1467–1504 — rising climatic seasonality pushed foragers into storage and sedentism, the precondition for farming and surplus; grounds the chapter’s “geography and climate as master force” in recent data. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjae012]
Ashraf & Galor (2011), “Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch,” American Economic Review 101(5): 2003–2041 — the canonical empirical statement that, before 1800, technology and land raised population density rather than income per head. The frontier anchor for this chapter’s quantity-vs-quality yardstick, and the thread it hands to Chapter 7. [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]







NoteResearch in focus — Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019): a gravity model on cuneiform




Aim — to show that Bronze Age long-distance trade obeyed the same economic regularities as modern trade, and to use them to locate cities now lost.
Question — can a structural gravity model, fit to ancient merchant records, recover trade costs and even the geographic position of unknown trading posts?
Data & method — roughly 12,000 clay tablets from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh (early second millennium BCE), recording shipments between named cities; a structural gravity model in which trade falls with distance is fit to the recorded flows, and the locations of lost cities are estimated as the coordinates that best rationalise the trade pattern.
Findings — trade fell with distance just as the modern gravity equation predicts; the model recovers sensible trade costs and places several lost cities close to where independent historical guesses had put them, with a few testable new predictions.
Caveats — the data are one merchant network in one region and period, heavily weighted to tin and textiles; the gravity structure is imposed, not proven, and the city-location estimates are probabilistic.

Sources: Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu, “Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(3), 2019 [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009].








NoteResearch in focus — Ashraf & Galor (2011): the Malthusian regime, and why “success” meant numbers




Aim — to test the central prediction of the Malthusian model for the pre-industrial world: that productivity gains raised population, not living standards.
Question — across the long pre-1800 era, did better technology and land translate into higher income per head, or simply into more people?
Data & method — assembled cross-country data on population density and income for the pre-industrial period and related them to measures of technological and land productivity, testing the Malthusian mechanism.
Findings — places with better technology and more productive land supported denser populations but not higher income per head; prosperity was converted into numbers, exactly as Malthus predicted, until the regime broke around 1800.
Caveats — deep-history income and population figures are reconstructions with wide error bands; the result characterises the regime on average, not every local episode.

Sources: Ashraf & Galor, “Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch,” American Economic Review 101(5), 2011 [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]. The quantity-vs-quality distinction it formalises is the yardstick paid off at Chapter 7.




Questions for consideration
Essay / exam style — reward the four-questions toolkit and the live debate, not recall.

“Before prices, how can we know a ‘world economy’ existed?” Answer with Bronze Age evidence — the diffusion of goods, shared standards, and the direction of the ships.
“Integration creates fragility.” Assess this claim using the Late Bronze Age Collapse and the contraction of the Uruk world system.
The Harappans ran the Gulf trade, yet the Indus survives as “a bright spot in a thin record.” Explain how that thinness can support rather than undermine the claim that the record under-documents the East.
How much explanatory weight should climate carry in the end of the Harappan urban phase? Distinguish abrupt-forcing, gradual-hydrological, and multi-causal accounts.
“Was Bronze Age trade a market, or redistribution?” Use Mesopotamia (Polanyi) and the Kanesh tablet evidence (Barjamovic et al.) to frame both sides.







TipCross-cutting questions (collected at the end of the book)



The book closes with a bank of questions spanning several chapters. Those this chapter opens: - Quantity vs quality. This chapter introduces the distinction between aggregate (“more people”) and per-capita (“richer people”) success. Trace it through Chapter 3, Chapter 4 and Chapter 7: when is a big economy legitimately a rich one? - Measuring integration. Compare measuring integration by the diffusion of goods (this chapter) with measuring it by price convergence (Chapter 8): what does each method see that the other misses?

# 4. Discuss why "more people" did NOT mean "richer people" — the quantity-vs-quality

title: Appendix C — The centre of gravity, chapter by chapter
text:
The table
This appendix collects, in one place, the running verdict each chapter entered into evidence: where the centre of economic gravity sat in that period, how confident the reading is on direction and on scale separately, and the evidence that carries it. Read down the table and the spine of the book appears as one movement — Asia central for most of the arc, a European interruption of roughly two centuries, and a partial return. The Conclusion walks these verdicts and weighs how strong the “European dominance as anomaly” reading can be made.
Each row is the evidence the chapter argued for. “Where the centre sat” summarises the verdict. Direction and scale are graded separately, because they are separate claims: you can be sure which way the weight lay and quite unsure how much of it there was, and saying both is the point of the exercise. “Strongest evidence” names what carries the reading, and how much there is to carry it.

One cell carries a fifth entry. Chapter 7’s scale is marked deferred, because the series that would settle it is being rebuilt; the reason is set out below.

title: Appendix C — The centre of gravity, chapter by chapter
text:
Reading the table
Four things the table shows, and two of them are gaps.
First, the plateau and the dip. For six chapters the reading stays in the east; for three it swings hard to the west; in the last it begins to return. The European interruption was real and large, but it was an interruption in a longer pattern rather than the pattern itself.
Second, the book knows direction far better than it knows scale. Read the two grades as columns and the difference is plain. Direction is high in seven of the nine periods that return a verdict at all; scale is low in five of them and reaches high only in the final chapter. That is what the surviving evidence allows. Bullion movements, city sizes, the direction of a trade in slaves or cottons, the way a price gradient pulled: each of these tells you which way the weight lay, because each is directional by nature. None of them tells you how much. The pre-modern chapters therefore make a strong claim about where and a weak one about how large, and keeping the two apart is what this table is for.
Confidence does not rise across the book. It opens at not applicable, runs high on direction for three chapters, falls to moderate for the two silver chapters, goes unresolved at the turning point, and returns to high for the last three. What does improve, and only at the very end, is the scale column: Chapter 10 is the single row resting on a computed coordinate rather than an inference.
Third, two moves that were not a simple east–west pendulum. The centre’s pull in Chapter 3 ran north, from the Abbasid core to its slave-and-fur periphery, not east; and the decisive shift of Chapter 9 ran within the West, from London to New York, not toward Asia. A centre of gravity can move inside a region as well as between regions, and the table only reads as a clean arc if those two moves are kept in view.
Fourth, where the table is weak or silent, and why.

Chapters 5 and 6 each rest on one instrument. The silver-sink verdict of Chapter 5 is carried by the bullion flow alone, and the module’s own rule is that bullion indicates the centre without defining it. Chapter 6’s production verdict is carried by the Bairoch-type manufacturing estimates, and it holds for the production measure only: on welfare ratios the two ends of Eurasia had already parted by about 1700. Both chapters claim high confidence in their own text. On the scale used here, one instrument carrying a reading is moderate, and moderate is what the table records.
Chapter 7 is unresolved, and is left so deliberately. That the centre moved west is not in dispute. When it crossed is. The chapter’s text dates the move to 1850, its own shares figure puts the crossing in the middle 1860s, and the locator series that places the marker is being rebuilt. Until that work is finished no date and no magnitude can be entered without guessing, so none is. Read the figure’s placement of the turning point as provisional too.
The early and late rows are not marks on the same ruler. Chapters 1 to 6 scored aggregate weight; from Chapter 7 the measure that mattered became income per head. That switch was the Great Divergence itself, and the book announces it rather than hiding it, but it does mean a high grade in Chapter 4 and a high grade in Chapter 10 were awarded on different questions.
Chapter 1 is silent, and the silence is the finding. Its pair of not-applicables is not a gap in the evidence but a statement about the period: there was no connected system whose weight could be located, so the question had no meaning yet. Recording that is more useful than forcing a low grade onto a question nobody could ask.

This is a summary instrument, not a measured series. The vertical placements in the figure are stylised judgements drawn from each chapter’s verdict for Chapters 1 to 9, and the placements around the turning point are under revision; only Chapter 10’s modern decades rest on a computed centre of gravity (Quah). Treat the table as the book’s argument made auditable — every entry traceable to a chapter, and every grade traceable to the instruments behind it — rather than as a quantitative dataset.

title: Appendix D — How the numbers were made
text:
How urbanisation rates get made, and why two experts differ by a factor of three
Several of this book’s most quotable figures are not measurements. They are constructions: a coefficient applied to an area, a ratio inferred from a handful of texts, a total extrapolated from one surviving document. Where a chapter needs the finding but not the derivation, the derivation lives here, so that a reader who wants to know how confident to be can see the working.
The rule this appendix applies throughout: a number built by multiplying an uncertain quantity by an assumed coefficient inherits the uncertainty of both, and the range it spans is usually wider than the debate about it suggests.
The share of a population living in cities is one of the most-used numbers in economic history, and in the deep past it is manufactured rather than counted. Mesopotamia offers an unusually clean demonstration, because two respected reconstructions of the same society disagree by a factor of three and the disagreement is entirely methodological.
Robert McC. Adams, working from archaeological survey, estimated that by about 2400 BCE some 78 per cent of the Sumerian population lived in settlements larger than 40 hectares — an extraordinarily urbanised society by any pre-modern standard. Piotr Steinkeller, working from the place-names recorded in administrative texts, reached the opposite conclusion for Ur III Umma: 70 to 80 per cent of its people lived outside the city, where Adams’s survey figures implied about 25 per cent.
Neither is careless. Survey finds sites by walking the ground and reading potsherds, and in an alluvial floodplain small settlements are buried, scoured away or hidden under later silt, so survey systematically under-counts the countryside. Texts record the places an administration had reason to name, which is not the same as the places people lived. Emberling attributes part of the gap to the two methods covering different time spans and part to sites the survey simply missed.
The lesson generalises, and this book will need it repeatedly. An urbanisation rate is a ratio of two constructed quantities, and the method that built each one determines the answer. When Chapter 2 takes up the population of Pataliputra, the same problem appears in a different guise: there the disagreement is not between survey and texts but between two lines drawn on the same site plan.
One further figure from the same chapter is worth holding beside these. Tell Brak, in northern Syria some 750 kilometres from Uruk, had reached about 130 hectares of settled area before 3500 BCE, perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, and it was contemporary with the southern cities rather than derived from them. Any account that makes southern irrigation the cause of Mesopotamian urbanism has to explain the north as well.
Sources: Emberling, “Mesopotamian cities and urban process, 3500-1600 BCE”, in The Cambridge World History, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 253-78, at pp. 271-72 for the Adams and Steinkeller figures and his account of the discrepancy, p. 275 for Ur at not much more than 50 hectares while the Wool Office employed some 13,000 workers, p. 262 for Tell Brak, and p. 255 for dry farming constraining northern cities to roughly 100 hectares until Neo-Assyrian irrigation.
Chapter 1 keeps the finding — that urbanisation rates are constructions rather than observations, and that two careful scholars can differ by a factor of three — and sends the derivation here.

title: Appendix D — How the numbers were made
section: How big was Pataliputra? A number and its pedigree
text:
How big was Pataliputra? A number and its pedigree
Figures between 40,000 and 400,000 circulate for Mauryan Pataliputra. Following one of them back is a short course in how ancient quantities are made.
The chain begins with Megasthenes, the Seleucid ambassador to Chandragupta, who described the city in his Indica. That book is lost. What survives are passages quoted by Strabo and Arrian centuries later, and the version most often cited is McCrindle’s translation of 1877. Through them Megasthenes gives dimensions: a parallelogram some eighty stadia long and fifteen broad, girded by a timber wall with 570 towers and sixty-four gates, and a ditch that doubled as the sewer.
Converted, that is roughly nine miles by two. But converted into what area? Here the estimates part company, and by more than is usually admitted. Allchin offers two: about 2,200 hectares for the outer rampart circuit, or about 340 hectares for the ground enclosed by the city moat. Erdosy gives a rampart-based range topping out at 1,350 hectares — often quoted alongside the others as if it were a third independent survey, which it is not. And Allchin reports Erdosy again, at 4,500 hectares, for the area Megasthenes’s description actually implies.
The last step is a density assumption. The standard coefficient is 120 persons per hectare — a figure Robert McC. Adams derived for Mesopotamia, and which Erdosy then imported into South Asia. Multiply it out and the arithmetic is unforgiving:

Nothing separates these answers except a decision about which line on the ground counts as the city. Same lost text, same translation, same coefficient, same modern authorities cited at more than one point on the range — and a spread of about thirteen to one. It is worth being clear what that does to the figures in general circulation: the familiar “about 200,000” needs no unaudited source to explain it, because it falls inside a range the held literature generates on its own. Shonaleeka Kaul, writing the Cambridge World History study of the city, takes the moat figure and concludes that “well over 40,000” people lived there, calling even that conservative.
Set against this, what has actually been dug is a thin record. Pataliputra lies beneath modern Patna; dense settlement and a high water table have kept excavation to fragments. The wooden palisade at Bulandibagh — plausibly Megasthenes’ wall — has been traced for about 350 feet. There is a burnt pillared hall at Kumrahar whose function is disputed three ways. That is the physical record for the greatest city in India.
None of this means the city was small. Every comparison in the table below survives the uncertainty, because the same conventions were applied to all of them, and on any reading Pataliputra was far larger than any other South Asian city of its day. It means that the number is an artefact of method, and that a book which quotes one figure without its boundary assumption has told you less than it appears to.

That c. 85 hectares is Kaul and Allchin’s own comparator, on their own convention, which is what makes the column internally consistent. It is not the figure Chapter 1 uses: there Mohenjo-daro is above 200 hectares, in the same class as Uruk rather than a third of it. The two numbers measure different things — an occupied mound against a wider site extent — so the cross-period comparison inherits a boundary problem at both ends, and cannot carry a precise multiple.

title: Appendix E — The disputes in full
text:
F Chapter 1 — Deep structures
Where a chapter stages a live scholarly disagreement, it keeps the finding and sends the argument here. Nothing in this appendix is settled; that is the point of it. A reader who wants only the state of play can stay in the chapters, and a reader who wants to know why the state of play is unsettled will find the reasons below.
The appendix is organised by chapter, so that each chapter’s live disagreements sit together and the apparatus grows with the book rather than being retro-fitted to it.

title: Appendix E — The disputes in full
text:
Indus governance, three ways
The three positions run as a spectrum rather than a quarrel. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer argues for rulers of a kind, reading the weight system as established by those rulers, plausibly for taxation — but he writes of the “so-called priest-king” himself and argues for several competing elite classes rather than a single sovereign. Gregory Possehl denies a state in the archaic sense, with no king and no royal apparatus, but affirms elites, ranks and a social pyramid, with authority perhaps sitting in councils. Adam Green goes further than either, arguing for collective governance in which many intersecting institutions rather than any ruling class coordinated labour and produced the public goods: the water infrastructure, the large non-residential buildings, the planning itself.
The evidence Green leans on hardest is the distribution of the seals. More than a thousand were recovered from the excavated areas of Mohenjo-daro alone, and on Franke-Vogt’s analysis the great majority came from ordinary households rather than large public structures. If seals recorded claims on resources, the right to make such claims was spread very widely.
That inference is where the dispute actually sits. The step from where seals were found to how the society was governed is an inference rather than a finding, and Possehl reads the same distribution as a concentration in particular quarters rather than a random spread. Weights may have been used in taxation, and at Harappa some were found by a neighbourhood gateway, though that has only been reported preliminarily and does not hold across sites. What was taxed, and by whom, is unknown.
What the three agree on is enough to carry the economic argument without settling the dispute, and that is why Chapter 1 does not try to settle it.

title: Appendix E — The disputes in full
text:
Why the Indus cities emptied
Four readings are in play, and the chapter takes none of them as settled.
Abrupt climate forcing. Staubwasser and colleagues, and Gupta and colleagues, treat the 4.2 ka event — a weakening of the monsoon around 2200 BCE — as the trigger. The difficulty is arithmetic: the de-urbanisation is dated around 1900 BCE, three centuries later, and a mono-causal climate account has to explain that lag away.
Gradual hydrological change. Giosan and colleagues emphasise rivers shifting and drying over generations rather than a single sharp drought. This fits the palaeoclimate record better, which shows no drought of the right timing and depth to topple a civilisation.
Internal, ideological failure. Gregory Possehl rejects environmental causation outright and reaches for a failure of whatever held the civilisation together. His is an ideological explanation, not a meteorological one.
Flooding routed through politics. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer keeps the water in the story but makes the causal link political: the rivers moved, the disruption was real, and what broke was the legitimacy of the people who had claimed to manage such things.
Two observations cut across all four. Both standard authorities attribute the drying of the Sarasvati or Ghaggar-Hakra system to tectonic change rather than monsoon failure, which detaches the most-cited piece of hydrological evidence from the climate story altogether. And on every reading, “de-urbanisation” fits the evidence better than “collapse”: the cities were given up, the population shifted east toward the Ganges, and the people did not disappear.
1
1 Sources: Possehl, The Indus Civilization (2002), for the rejection of environmental causation and the ideological reading; Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998), for flooding mediated by a crisis of legitimacy, and both for the tectonic account of the Sarasvati; Staubwasser et al. and Gupta et al. for abrupt forcing; Giosan et al. for gradual hydrological change.

title: Appendix E — The disputes in full
text:
Redistribution versus market at Uruk
Polanyi placed a redistributive pattern at the heart of the early Near East, and Uruk’s state textile workshops — credited with as many as 9,000 women — are the exhibit usually offered for it. Three things complicate that.
The chronology. The archives documenting administered redistribution most fully are Ur III, around 2100 BCE, more than a millennium after Uruk. Emberling treats the great collection-and-redistribution centres as an innovation of that empire rather than a feature of the first cities — and Scott, the source of the 9,000 figure, writes in the same passage that reading such evidence back to the Uruk period “is highly questionable”.
The strongest version has been walked back. The “temple-city” model, built on the archive of the temple of Ba’u at Lagash, held that temples owned essentially everything. Continued study of that same archive showed it had dramatically overstated how much land one temple held, and the Ba’u estate turns out to have been supervised by the queens of Lagash rather than by a priesthood standing apart from the palace.
Emberling is more deflationary still: markets, walls and temples cannot be used to explain why cities arose, because none of them developed fully until later.
What survives into the chapter is the position it takes: redistribution and market dealing coexisted, and the balance between them is contested rather than settled. The Uluburun cargo, a thousand years later, shows both running in the same hold.

title: Appendix E — The disputes in full
text:
The Phoenician metals question
The commercial thesis, argued at length by Susan Frankenstein and developed by Maria Eugenia Aubet, holds that the western settlements were commercial factories and that the whole diaspora was a response to Assyrian pressure on Tyre. The mining frontiers do open when the model predicts, in south-western Spain and at Laurion in the Aegean.
The case against is archaeological, and it is not that the metals trade did not happen but that it does not explain the settlements. The excavated colonies look like farms. They were agricultural towns from their foundation — wine and salted fish at Huelva by the eighth century, Gadir buying farmland across the bay around 800 BCE — and at ninth- and eighth-century Huelva, of some eight thousand potsherds, 99.9 per cent are local or Phoenician and fewer than fifty are Greek. Nathan Pilkington puts the negative sharply: the implication that Iberian metals were destined for Near Eastern markets cannot, he argues, be corroborated from the archaeological record. The Phoenicians never permanently settled the Atlantic tin coasts and abandoned the stations they did place there, and a direct run from Tyre to Gadir was some four and a half thousand kilometres and a month’s sailing, which allows one voyage a season.
Where the field has moved is easy to overstate in either direction. The older scholarship explained the colonies exclusively by trade in metals. The newer work, with specialised settlements, survey, archaeobotany and archaeometallurgy, has opened the explanation to territorial, productive and social motives alongside the commercial one. That is a broadening, not a refutation.
What would settle it: provenance work tying the silver in Levantine hoards to Iberian ores. This book has not found that evidence either way.
2

On the Phoenician question, Lopez-Ruiz and Doak (eds), The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean (2019), and Pilkington, The Carthaginian Empire, p. 61.
